idea.title: Scaffold for hd-20261002-190816-acbca5c51921/candidates/0/1/idea/1
idea.description: IDEA: Build a "change-intent ledger" that records why a platform change was made (the hypothesis, expected metric movement, rollback trigger) alongside the diff, then automatically compares outcomes to the stated intent weeks later, so platform teams learn which kinds of changes actually pay off.
idea.problem_framing: Find meaningful software opportunities for a developer platform team.
assumptions: Developers will state intent in structured form if it takes under 30 seconds; this may fail if it feels like extra ceremony, and stated intents may be written vaguely enough to be unfalsifiable.
Consumer usage data is complete enough to build the graph; shadow consumers (scripts, notebooks, cron jobs, external partners) may be invisible and could dominate the real risk.
Observability coverage is sufficient to infer actual dependencies; sampled traces may miss rare but critical paths.

Behavioral friction signals correlate with real productivity loss; some waiting is productive (thinking, review), and instrumenting developers raises trust and privacy concerns that could cause backlash.
Platform teams will act on the data; the bottleneck may be prioritization or ownership rather than lack of insight.
Divergence is mostly informative rather than noise; teams may diverge for legitimate reasons that the detector would misclassify as problems.
Runbooks can be expressed or extracted into executable steps; many involve judgment, credentials, or production-only state that cannot be safely sandboxed.
Agent usage inside the organization is, or soon will be, high enough to justify dedicated infrastructure; existing IAM and audit systems might already be adequate with minor extensions.
Tagging and ownership data are accurate enough for attribution; shared infrastructure may make cost allocation inherently contested.

Build a "change-intent ledger" that records why a platform change was made (the hypothesis, expected metric movement, rollback trigger) alongside the diff, then automatically compares outcomes to the stated intent weeks later, so platform teams learn which kinds of changes actually pay off.

Create a "deprecation pressure simulator" that models the downstream effect of retiring an internal API, library version, or pipeline step by sampling real consumer call graphs, then outputs a ranked, probabilistic migration plan with confidence ranges rather than a single date.

Build an "environment drift archaeologist" that diffs what a service believes about its runtime (declared config, IaC, docs) against observed behavior (traces, network flows, actual dependencies) and surfaces the discrepancies as a ranked backlog.

Unconventional alternative: rather than building more self-service tooling, build a "friction sensor" that passively measures where developers wait, retry, or abandon workflows (CI reruns, repeated failed deploys, docs searches that end in a Slack question) and treats that signal as the product roadmap.

Build a "golden path decay detector" that tracks how far teams have diverged from the recommended templates and flags divergences that are either a risk (security or compliance drift) or an unmet need (a signal the template should evolve).

Create a "flaky-knowledge" tool for internal docs and runbooks that tests them: executes sandboxed steps from runbooks in ephemeral environments on a schedule and reports which instructions no longer work.

Build an "AI-agent traffic governor" for the platform: a layer giving coding agents scoped, auditable, rate-limited access to internal tools, with per-agent budgets and a replayable record of what each agent did and why.
Build a "cost-to-intent" attribution layer that maps cloud and CI spend to product-level outcomes and teams, with what-if estimates ("moving this job to spot instances saves X with Y% failure risk").
